Shov Sha-Rushman was the first one to effectively mathematise economic speculation, developing a number of proposed relationships between variables. As a leading figure in the 'third wave' of economic speculation, he would be a key figure in economic orthodoxy.

Dhofmazhi Zhakd was a major correspondent with Shov Sha-Rushman, and a major newspaper man in Gaubja. He was a major populariser of Rushmanian economic thought, as well as a member of the Gaubjan economic reform league.

Hwamp Puur was a major critic of the quickly established orthodoxy of Sha-Rushman's thought. He challenged the notion that economics was representable by a priori methods such as mathematics, and commited himself to a descriptivist and empiricist account of economics.

Dhomak M‚zfa was the first thinker to seriously apply the functionalist philosophy to economic thought, which gave birth to the 'operationist' school of economics. Trade, to some extent, as it did very little beyond move things around, became nearly immaterial to what consisted of 'the economy'. M‚zhfa priortised studying factors of production.

Mobauk Mizava was a desciple of Dhomak M‚zfa. He extended M‚zfa's analysis of 'pure growth' to a larger 'thermodynamic' energic system, where he declared the only fit subject of economics was the study of the sun, solar energy, and other heaveny things which appear to produce their own energy.

B‚zajopt Kushkt was the first statist theorist of economics. He suggest that the state take control of all factors of production to ensure proper management, and reduce 'unreal' phenomena like trade distorition created by speculators and retailers.

Dimash Kushkt was the brother of the more famous B‚zajopt Kushkt, and a close desciple of his. He studied living conditions in industrial slums in Bagh, and provided his brother with the data that he would use to argue that state control of factors of production would reduce both the suffering of the common man and increase efficiency.

Bida Fovkazh was a factory manager in Jiishan‚g who quickly adopted functionalist-statist principles in his operation. By refusing to sell a large number of his goods and rendering them directly to his workers, and attempting to set up an autarkic system, he was a pioneer of the statist cartel firms that would so trouble governments in the early 14th century.

Yomeg Og Yezoz was a Takemogine longshoreman who worked in the dockywards in Seikaukz. Exposed to functionalist and statist critiques, he attempted to agitate both the government and his employers to do more for the working industrial classes. He would later join the parliament as the first electee of the Takemogi statist party.

Makoun Sha-Gosod Sha-Man, a scion of the illustrious Poumnian aristocratic house of Sha-Gosod Sha-Man, which would also produce the later, better known Vufo Sha-Gosod Sha-Man, agitated by what he described as 'demotic' and 'sickeningly plebian gashdzoun thinking' economic thought, especially statism, described an economic system where he believed that there were naturally aristocratic classes in every society and economic, and natural slave peoples, and there was no point in reforming the economy.

Droum Sha-Mushim was an economist of the school of what would come to be called the 'organical school'. The organical school emphasised the historical and cultural development of economic systems, drawing on the work of Hwamp Puur.

JÍbun Yannagath was an organicist economist from the Rannu Empire. He criticised the industrial developement in society and was a major interpreter of Tehuhrite law in context of modern economic developments.

Foda Nagjoni was a numismatician, who complied a large catalogue of the history of coinage in Ishahfazh. His work incidentally contained a number of monetary theories, grounded in organicist thinking.

Shrumu Mruuwun was another major member of the organistic school. Long a professor in the Studium of Prousorum, his works on value largely gradually descended into apologetics for the Poumnian regime.
Druut Sha-Mang was a major theorist of war economy, and public financing. He studied historical methods of loan raising by governments, and became an early theoretician of trust.
Nokodopau Vokuma was a Vokonazhi aristocrat and planter, who became an early agronomist, as well as a reactionary advocate, describing a paternalistic and pastoralist 'folk economy'.

Vufo Sha-Gosod Sha-Man was a highly influential economist, who may be said to be the 'economist of empire'. Suggesting that large, self suficient economic blogs can run up colossal debts to finance imperial wars, he justified the arms race of the late 14th century by appeal to high government debt spending as a drive of demand and economic growth.
Guabjim Fauzhkt was the first finance minister of the N‚gine absolutist government. He advocated for large scale printing of money to finance the various nagine war efforts.

Buro Tugot-So was a major member of the Athisoroon parliament's 'tarrif party'. He advocated repeatedly raising tarrifs, and borrowing and spending extensively, in accordance with the Gosodian school.

Masogu Foma-So was one of the few dissenting voices in the heydey of Godosian economics. By clining to a liberationist economy, grounded in organically acting small producers, and echewing debt, he was a relict of the organicist school.
Fimpo Sha-Pomp was one of the few poumnian adopters of operationalism. He was a major student of production efficency and economy of scale.

The instituional school was one of the most developed economic schools of the 14th century. It was centered around the person and work of Dhom‚mak Maptazh, who argued that instituions, customs, and states shape markets, as well as market behaviour. His rationalistic method allowed for a great degree of study of many topics within an institutionalist paradigm.

Mazupt Pazhkash was a major student of marginality. He came to this in fact in terms of studying 'losses' incurred in taxation, by the tax payer, in his studies of the effects of taxation on market behaviour.
Boddamag Gidazh was an important student of social behaviour and consumption. His studies bled into sociology. He was a professor at the studium of Nozho.

Wroushou Tzamutzi was one of the first complete student of markets: how they come into being, the different sorts of markets (e.g. thin vs thick) and how markets take on definite characters related to trust and regulation.
Kib Mroud was a Poumnian exponent of the instituional school. He drew on the work of the precursors of the instituional school, especially his countryman Voun Sha-Pomid.
Zadak Optazh was an instituionalist student of household economics. He studied the reasons everyday persons make economic choices.

Mahdmaut Maktazh was an instituionalist student of the role of technological development in economic growth: the role of research in accounting for gaps in traditional economic theory's explanation of the astounding growth that came with industrialisation.
Pruudum Sha-Trunguntwu was a theorist of economic epistemology: how the economic of information effects economic choices and behaviour.

Orumuu Vorid was a theorist of land usage. Particularly, he connected theories of marginality to land usage, and suggested reasons for colonial expansions were a consequence of increasingly poor returns on occupying new land in a given land market.
Middanak Doshkva was a theorist of the sociology of business enterprises and their role in shaping consumption patterns. He studied avaliability and substituion.
P‚azahpt Dazhpt was a theorist of market cycles. He attempted to understand why crashes happened, and came to the conclusion that they were driven by excessive production.
Nobamedes Zhakdi was a theorist of market cycles. He attempted to understand why crashes happened, and came to the conclusion that they were driven by limits to the money supply.
Mraakunt Sha-Mong was a theorist of historical technological growth. He suggested that thin markets were vulnerable to knowledge loss.

The fourteenth century witnessed tremendous advances in the capacity for explosive distruction. An era that had started with little more advanced than simple black powder would, at the end of it, have seen the advent of both plastic explosives and nitroglycerin.

The design and production of basic munitions saw much improvement over the course of the fourteenth century. Advances in weapons design -- from muzzle to breech loads to semi-automatics and machine guns -- naturally meant that the design and production of ammunition also had to follow suit.

The industrial revolution of the fourteenth century affected practically all areas of hominid endeavour, and the production of artillery was no exception. What had previously been a lengthy process of cast molding bronze cannons would -- in the hands of luminaries of the industry, such as the technicians of the Sha-Shoumid firm -- become an industrialized and exact sience.

With the inventions of breech loaded rifles, mechanized rifle drilling, semi-automatics, and other technical improvements in weapons design, the industrial output of small arms was vastly increased during the fourteenth century.
